question: The heatwave that has affected Europe since June 2026 illustrates the worsening risks associated with climate change. According to the World Health Organisation, it had already caused more than 1 000 deaths by 30 June 20261. Eurostat figures show that annual household energy consumption for cooling has almost doubled in the EU since 2015. While cooling still accounted for only 0.

8% of the EU’s final energy consumption in 20242, heatwaves are driving up electricity demand, putting increasing pressure on energy grids and markets. As Europe gets hotter, air conditioning is becoming less and less about comfort and more a public health issue of protecting the most vulnerable.

As a consequence, we need to adapt buildings to cope with heatwaves, encourage the installation of efficient, energy-saving airconditioning systems – alongside passive cooling solutions – and ensure that the electricity infrastructure can meet the growing demand for cooling.
Does the Commission intend to support Member States in developing sustainable airconditioning solutions and adapting electricity grids to meet the foreseeable increase in cooling needs?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.10.2026) The Commission supports Member States to deploy sustainable cooling solutions and to upgrade the electricity grids to face increased cooling needs. The Grids Action Plan1 and the European Grids package2 upgrade and accelerate the roll-out of electricity grids. The Connecting Europe Facility delivers direct financial support3.

The Electrification Action Plan4 emphasises the role of efficient electrification, including in cooling of buildings and deployment of heat pumps. The upcoming Cooling and Heating Action Plan will address the growing need for efficient cooling.

The Energy Performance of Buildings Directive5 encourages holistic approaches integrating multiple solutions such as reduction of internal heat gain, solar shading and insulation to keep heat out, and ventilative cooling as well as active cooling6.

The Commission also supports climate responsive building design, including passive cooling techniques and nature-based solutions, for example through the New European Bauhaus7 and technical guidance on climate resilient buildings8 and green roofs9.

With specific reference to cooling needs, the Commission has relevant tools, such as the EUfunded update of the World Health Organization guidance on heat-health action plans10, the Guidelines on climate adaptation11, know-how via the European Climate and Health Observatory12, guidance13 and online tools14 for employers and workplaces.
